title: Measuring Whether Jailbreaks That Succeed Once Reliably Succeed on Retry
original_idea: For each of 30 harmful prompts tested with 3 attack methods on 2 models, repeat each attack attempt 10 times at temperature 1.0 and record whether each attempt succeeds. Compute per-prompt reliability (fraction of 10 attempts that succeed) and plot its distribution.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Directly informs defense design: if jailbreaks are unreliable, retry-limit defenses work; if reliable, they do not. Practical deployment implications.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Conceptually simple: run the same prompts multiple times and count successes. Requires implementing 3 attack methods, but the analysis is straightforward. Medium compute handles repeated runs.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: 30 prompts x 3 attacks x 2 models x 10 retries. That is 1800 inference calls, which is a lot but the experimental design is tight. Clear deliverable.

novelty.reasoning: JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) uses greedy decoding for targets but temperature 1 for attackers, acknowledging stochasticity. StrongREJECT (BAIR 2024) examines single-turn attacks with and without retries. Multi-turn jailbreak research reports 90-99% ASR on open-weight models. However, no published work systematically measures per-prompt reliability distributions (fraction of 10 attempts that succeed per prompt) and plots the distribution. The specific question of whether jailbreaks are deterministic or stochastic at the per-prompt level, with temperature 1.0 retry distributions, remains a gap.
